Lucas Heidemann has worked since September 2019 at the Center for Acoustic and Thermal Building Physics of the Stuttgart University of Applied Sciences (HFT Stuttgart), but expected to register formally as a doctoral candidate only around mid-2023. In September 2022, universities of applied sciences (HAW) in Baden-Württemberg won the right to award doctorates through a joint doctoral association, following Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Saxony, with Berlin, Bavaria and Schleswig-Holstein close behind; the doctoral regulations were still being drafted.

Heidemann earned a bachelor’s degree in building physics at HFT in 2017 and a master’s in Sound and Vibration in Gothenburg, then took a post offered by Professor Berndt Zeitler, in whose group he had written his bachelor’s thesis. His applied research concerns impact sound insulation of thermally decoupled balconies: accepted engineering practice requires thermal connection elements in cantilevered balconies to prevent mold, and new impact-sound requirements have applied since 2018. He is developing a lab test procedure and a prediction method, and uses measurements and finite element simulations to improve low-frequency insulation.

The work belongs to iCity, a project funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) that has involved more than 50 HFT researchers and over 45 partners since 2017 in developing solutions for livable, intelligent and sustainable cities. Funding is secure, though industry partners’ needs do not always match his doctoral goals. He supervises student theses, works 80% so he can teach acoustics at the Ludwigsburg School of Musical Instrument Making, and expects the BW-CAR doctoral college, founded in 2014, to grow in importance.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from Lucas Heidemann’s first-person profile in Akustik Journal, published by the German Acoustical Society (DEGA).
